clue.text: I run important circuit the wrong way round, finishing-line providing some comfort

indicators.note: read as turning the first four pieces about; a strict reversal leaves the I out of place, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: to run is to race
vital means important
a lap is one circuit of a track

indicators.note: finishing points to the final letter of the word line

explanation.surface: An athlete runs a big race backwards towards the finishing line, which somehow gives comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The wrong way round' suggests a reversal, but read strictly backwards the lone I lands at the end, not after PALL, so only a rearrangement places every letter; 'finishing-line' then adds E.
explanation.definitionFit: Care given to ease pain and symptoms rather than cure them, as in a hospice, provides some comfort.

clue.text: Buzz Ira Gershwin's GP's number

indicators.note: buzz suggests letters set humming and jumbled, so the following words are rearranged

parts.note: used as written, its S included
used as written, its S included

explanation.surface: A message about the lyricist Ira Gershwin's doctor and their phone number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buzz' looks like a phone call to the GP's number; it signals the rearrangement of all fifteen letters. 'Number' is a song, as a performer's numbers are.
explanation.definitionFit: A number is a song in a show or set, and this 1940s ballad recorded by the Ink Spots is one.

clue.text: Only supplying basic facts in touring week on…

indicators.note: touring is travelling around, so these letters wander into a new order

parts.note: the dots join this clue to 4 Down, whose answer is the word this in that clue refers to, so it joins the fodder

explanation.surface: A tour guide who gives only the bare facts while on tour for a week.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots run on into 4 Down, whose 'this' is that clue's own answer; DONT, from 4 Down, is the last part of the anagram fodder. The phrase comes from the 2 Down song.
explanation.definitionFit: Information given on a strictly essential basis supplies only the facts a person must have and nothing more.

clue.text: …this stop in Stratford on travels!

indicators.note: in says the letters sit within the words Stratford on travels

explanation.surface: A traveller makes a stop in Stratford-upon-Avon while on the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'StratforD ON Travels'. 'This' points back to 3 Down, where this answer is part of the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouted as an order, the contraction of do not tells someone to stop what they are doing.

clue.text: Everything he related about nights abroad: 22 11 21D to 7 13D?

parts.note: all means everything

indicators.note: about says the word related wraps around he

parts.note: related, as of a story, means told
taken as written

indicators.note: abroad means scattered widely, so the letters of nights are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man tells everything about his nights spent overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reads as a song line, WHY TELL THEM ... TO THE TREES?, which this phrase completes; the words come from the 2 Down lyric.
explanation.definitionFit: In the song, the grass is asked why it repeats old stories and memories to the trees; this is the missing phrase.

clue.text: Part of campsite where change may be had for Spooner's capital?…

indicators.note: Spooner's says the opening sounds of two words are swapped

parts.note: change is loose cash
a tent is one part of a campsite

explanation.surface: At a festival campsite, a tent where you can get change for money.
explanation.walkthrough: The swap turns CASH TENT into TASH KENT.
explanation.definitionFit: This city is the capital of Uzbekistan in Central Asia.

clue.text: Different men clearing perimeter? It's definite

indicators.note: clearing a perimeter strips away a word's outside letters, here given by men

parts.note: different means other
OR, other ranks, is an abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Some unusual men clearing a fence line, and someone is certain about it.
explanation.walkthrough: OR (other ranks, soldiers) are removed from both ends of OTHER, leaving three letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar this little word is called a definite article, as opposed to a or an, which are indefinite.

clue.text: …another turning heads in business circles — JR?

indicators.note: circles means goes round, so one piece is placed around another

parts.note: on, as in a deal being on, means going ahead in business

indicators.note: turning heads swaps the opening pair of letters of the word round, so the first moves behind the second

parts.note: another follows on from 6 Across: another capital city, Lima, capital of Peru

explanation.surface: A tycoon turning heads among business people, like a famous television character.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots link back to 6 Across, so 'another' means another capital. 'Turning heads' turns only LI to give ILMA, which ON circles.
explanation.definitionFit: JR Ewing, villain of the TV soap Dallas, was a Texas petroleum tycoon.

clue.text: Soaks tracking friend on path, head down: 4 11 21D to 7 13D?

indicators.note: tracking means following behind, so this piece comes after

parts.note: an ally is a friend

indicators.note: head down sends a word's first letter to its bottom, since this is a down entry

parts.note: a course is a path
to ret flax is to soak it, so rets means soaks

explanation.surface: Drunkards following a friend down a path with their heads lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head down' moves the C of COURSE to the end, giving OURSEC. The definition is a song line from 2 Down, DON'T TELL THEM ... TO THE TREES?
explanation.definitionFit: The song begs the grass not to pass on private confidences to the trees; this phrase fills the gap.

clue.text: Uncomfortable cox settled for what's literally restrictive

indicators.note: uncomfortable suggests things out of place, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rowing cox sits uneasily in the boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uncomfortable' looks like a description of the cox, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A document available only to a restricted readership limits who may read its words, so its letters are literally restricted.

clue.text: Box not quite fitting order

indicators.note: not quite means falling short by a final letter

parts.note: the box is British slang for a television, the telly

explanation.surface: A box that does not quite fit the order it was meant for.
explanation.definitionFit: To instruct someone to do something is to order them.

clue.text: Honour new path taken from behind summerhouse

indicators.note: taken from behind means read starting at the back

parts.note: the OBE is a British honour
a zag is a sharp turn onto a new path

explanation.surface: A newly honoured person laying a fresh path round the back to the summerhouse.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden pavilion with a view, often a summerhouse, is a common English garden feature.

clue.text: Quixote, for example, admits a little compilation's hastily attached…

indicators.note: admits means lets something inside

parts.note: Don Quixote, the deluded knight of Cervantes's novel, was a Spanish don who took on windmills

indicators.note: a little means just a first letter

explanation.surface: Don Quixote's story gets a small anthology bolted on in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: Quixote is a 'take-don' because he took on giants, which were really windmills.
explanation.definitionFit: Something added as an afterthought, roughly fixed on, has been quickly fastened to the rest.

clue.text: My colleague's outside right for Forest?

indicators.note: outside means placed around

parts.note: Tees is another Independent setter, a colleague of Nimrod

explanation.surface: A fellow footballer playing outside right for Nottingham Forest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside right' is an old football position, but 'outside' is the container signal and 'right' gives R.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest is a great mass of woodland, so a plural of wooded plants fits it, the question mark marking the loose fit.

clue.text: Guarantee draughtsman's tip has been snatched by scoundrel

indicators.note: tip has been snatched by says the last letter of one word is taken into the next

parts.note: a chequer is a piece in draughts
a cad is a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A rogue steals the pen tip of an architect's draughtsman.
explanation.walkthrough: The R at the tip of CHEQUER is snatched into CAD, giving CHEQUE and CARD. 'Draughtsman' looks like a drawer of plans but is a piece in draughts.
explanation.definitionFit: Before debit cards, a bank card was shown with a cheque as a guarantee that the bank would honour it.

clue.text: …22 my colleague's reported method of transmission

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the pronunciation is what counts

parts.note: 22 Down gives the word for the reason, and Phi is a fellow Independent setter

explanation.surface: A setter's colleague reports on how a signal is sent.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots continue from 13 Across. PHI is another Independent setter.
explanation.definitionFit: Wireless networking is a way of sending data between devices by radio waves.

clue.text: Eccentricity suppressed by particular relation

indicators.note: suppressed by means held down inside

parts.note: nice can mean particular, fussy
e is the mathematical symbol for the eccentricity of a conic

explanation.surface: A particular relative keeps her odd behaviour under control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eccentricity' looks like odd behaviour, but in maths e stands for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A brother's or sister's daughter is a family relation.

clue.text: Activity of rogue flier?

definitions.meaning: a prank or bit of mischief, the kind of thing a rascal gets up to
a songbird that rises singing high into the sky

explanation.surface: A rogue pilot gets up to something.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a bit of fun or mischief and a small songbird famous for its high song.

clue.text: Numbers worn by past women

indicators.note: worn by means carried around the body, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: tens are numbers
ago means in the past

explanation.surface: Outfits that women wore in earlier times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Numbers' is a fashion word for outfits, as in a little black number, and also gives TENS.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose afternoon dresses were fashionable among Victorian and Edwardian ladies for taking afternoon refreshment at home.

clue.text: Loose holy woman losing head wants God back briefly

indicators.note: losing head means dropping the first letter

parts.note: a nun is a holy woman

indicators.note: back means read in reverse
briefly means cut short by the last letter

parts.note: a deity is a god

explanation.surface: A nun loses her mind and wants her god back for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: NUN without its head gives UN; DEITY shortened is DEIT, which turned back gives TIED.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfastened knots and laces are loose.

clue.text: Finally, murder charge revoked — Queen famously surviving

indicators.note: revoked is taken as turned back

parts.note: a rap is a criminal charge

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of murder

explanation.surface: A murder charge is finally dropped, and the queen survives.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine, Henry VIII's sixth wife, outlived him, as the rhyme says: divorced, beheaded, died; divorced, beheaded, survived.

clue.text: We'll go around with tricorns barking

definitions.text: We'll go around with tricorns barking

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, so these letters are mixed up

parts.note: only the we of we'll is used; the will is part of the surface

explanation.surface: Town officials in three-cornered hats shouting as they make their rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' is both the shouting and the anagram signal; the WE from 'We'll' joins TRICORNS.
explanation.definitionFit: Bell-ringing public announcers traditionally wore tricorn hats and walked the streets calling out news.

clue.text: Opposition to US ambassador staying in Turkmenistan

indicators.note: staying in means lodged inside

parts.note: TM is the country code for Turkmenistan
an ambassador is addressed as His Excellency, HE

explanation.surface: An American ambassador posted in Turkmenistan, facing opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like the United States but is the pronoun us.
explanation.definitionFit: In the phrase us and them, the other side is the opposing group.

clue.text: The reason a letter is read aloud

indicators.note: read aloud means the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: the twenty-fifth letter of the alphabet is Y

explanation.surface: Someone asks why a letter is being read out.
explanation.definitionFit: Asking for the cause or purpose of something is asking for its reason.

clue.text: I'll get cuddled by Judge, being a pansy

indicators.note: get cuddled by means held inside

parts.note: esse is Latin for being, as in in esse
I'll gives I, the will a link to the surface

explanation.surface: A judge gets a hug and is called a softie.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang this is a weak or effeminate man, a mild insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are dated British slang for a soft, unmanly man, a weakling.

clue.text: Make delivery on circuit where there's a RAM reserve

parts.note: in cricket, to york a batsman is to bowl a yorker, a delivery pitched at the feet
a logic gate is an electronic circuit

explanation.surface: A delivery van on a round to a farm where rams are kept in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: RAM is the Royal Academy of Music, whose museum is at York Gate by Regent's Park in London; it is not a male sheep or computer memory.
explanation.definitionFit: This London address beside Regent's Park houses the Royal Academy of Music's museum and collections.
